name: term-sheet-powers
of: Mechanisms by which a term in a financing carries power beyond its price, each named with the future state in which it bites, who holds the power when that state arrives, and the case in which the term proved worthless or fatal, including terms whose only cash value is the price of their own waiver and terms exercised by a holder who never signed them.
items: Dividend in the drawer: a cumulative dividend that is never paid accrues into the preference, so the claim on an exit grows with the calendar and with nothing else, as an eight percent cumulative on a growth round turns a one-times preference into roughly one and two-thirds after seven years while the common's share of the same sale shrinks each year the company does not sell; not the preference itself but its slope in time, worthless in the fast rich exit where the preferred converts and fatal in the slow modest one, where the years bought by patience were paid out of the common.

Redemption clock: after a stated number of years the preferred may demand its money back, which bites only in the state where the company is alive, unsold, and unable to raise, and there it is rarely a claim on cash, since a Delaware company may redeem only from funds legally available and the board decides what those are, as the ThoughtWorks investors learned when their demand yielded a determination rather than a payment; the power is not the money but the standing to put the company in default, which is then sold back as forbearance.

Threshold that quietly disenfranchises: information rights, pro rata, and the rest are granted to a major investor defined by a share count or a dollar figure, so every later round that dilutes a holder below the line strips its powers by arithmetic rather than by any vote, as the seed fund that learns of the sale from the press because it fell out of the definition two rounds earlier; not a term with a bite of its own but the key that decides who holds the others, and its holder is whoever writes the next definition.

Claim on the middle: a one-times non-participating preference exists only for exits between the preference and the point where converting to common pays more, since at the top it converts and adds nothing and at zero it is a claim on nothing, as the stack of preferences that exceeds a company's realistic sale price leaves the common underwater and makes the acquirer buy the management back with a carve-out plan; not downside protection, which would pay at the bottom, but a claim on the modal exit that nobody at signing rehearses.

Flat where the founder is steep: in the band where the preferred's payoff is flat, from the preference up to the conversion point for non-participating stock and from the cap up to it for capped participation, the preferred gains nothing from a higher price while the common's payoff is at its steepest, so a holder with a vote on the sale prefers the certain offer now to a better one later, as when the investors accept an acquirer's price inside the flat band and the founders, whose every extra dollar would be theirs, are dragged; not the size of the claim but its slope, and an uncapped participating preferred has the claim without the flatness.

Stack that sorts the syndicate: seniority among series decides who is paid first in the middling exit and so sorts the investors into parties with different preferences over the same sale, since the senior holder is whole at any price above its own preference and the junior is paid only above the whole stack, as when the later fund's senior preference makes it a seller at a price at which the earlier fund is a holdout; not investor against founder but the rules of a fight among investors, which the founder signs and later meets as a board that cannot agree to sell.

Chair that owes the room: a board seat is a vote that matters only when the board is split, a place at the information every month, and a duty that runs to the common as residual claimant rather than to the fund that appointed the director, so in the middling exit where the preference takes the price and the common takes nothing the seat becomes a liability in the very state it was taken for, as litigated in the Trados sale, where the preferred took the proceeds, the management plan took the rest, and the common took nothing; not control, since one seat controls nothing, but a channel that carries a duty against its holder, which is why a fund sometimes prefers the observer's chair, information without duty.

First to know it is dying: monthly financials and inspection rights are worth the lag between holders, since whoever learns first that the company is failing can stop reserving, mark down, sell a position, or decline the bridge before the others know it is needed, as the major investor who passes on the rescue it was first to see coming while the holders below the threshold find out at the wash-out; not a power over the company but a power relative to the other holders, and worthless in the company that never sends the reports and is never made to, which is most companies until the state arrives.

Pass that stamps the sale: a right of first refusal on transfers, held by the parties who also hold the information, makes every secondary sale a signal, since the outside buyer knows the insiders saw the numbers and passed, so the founder or angel who needs liquidity finds the outsider's price discounted by the insiders' refusal and the insiders able to buy at that discount; not a price set for the stranger's eyes but a refusal read as one, and it bites hardest on the holder who needs the sale most.

Fired into the cliff: founder shares vest on a schedule the board can cut short by terminating the founder, and the voting agreement fixes the board that the founder's majority of common might otherwise unseat, so the cap table is changed by a personnel act rather than by a vote on shares, as the cofounder let go in the eleventh month whose unvested three quarters return to a pool the board controls; not a hold on pay still owed but a hold on ownership already granted, released or seized by whoever controls employment, and an acquirer's double trigger is the same term read from the other side.

Veto priced by the clock: protective provisions let a class block a sale, a senior round, or new debt, and the block is worth exactly what the blocked party's speed is worth, so the same veto is a formality in a cash-rich year and a power over survival with three weeks of runway, as the seed class that holds up the rescue round for a better conversion until the round dies; not the right to demand anything but the right to delay everything, and series-by-series votes multiply the vetoes while a single-class vote lets the large series override the small.

Option on the next round's information: pro rata is a call on the next round at the next round's price, worth the gap between what the insider knows and what the price reflects, so it is worth most in the oversubscribed round of a winner, where it crowds the new lead who wants the allocation, and nothing in the down round or in the hands of a fund with no reserves left to exercise it, as the seed fund whose whole return sat in the pro rata of two companies it could not afford to follow; not a promise of support but a free option granted as a courtesy, and its value concentrates exactly where the founder has the most alternatives.

Reserves test in loyalty's clothing: pay-to-play converts the preferred of any investor who does not fund its share of the down round into common, or strips its anti-dilution, so it bites on funds without reserves rather than on founders and sorts the syndicate by dry powder under the name of commitment, as the small seed fund in its eighth year whose entire position converts; not a founder's term at all, since the founder is an incidental beneficiary, but a term investors sign against each other while imagining they would always play.

Ratchet that must be waived: full-ratchet anti-dilution reprices the earlier round to the down round's price, and exercised as written it wipes the common, so the new lead refuses to fund a cap table with no management incentive, and the round the ratchet was written for is the round in which it must be waived; not protection against the down round but a chip that matures into it, and its whole value is the price of its own waiver, paid in a board seat, a fee, or a gentler formula.

Claim on terms not yet written: a most-favored-nation clause copies the best terms of any later instrument to every earlier holder, so a sweetener the desperate company offers one rescuer is multiplied across everyone who holds the clause, and the rescue that needed one sweetener cannot afford the propagated one; a term priced by a negotiation between two other parties that has not happened yet, and unlike the most-favored promise offered to break an impasse, its bite is the multiplier it becomes later.

Threshold that ends independence: drag-along names the coalition, usually the board plus a preferred majority, that can force every holder to sell, and it bites when the investors' clocks diverge from the company's, as the fund past its tenth year that needs distributions and pulls the drag at a price inside the stack where the common takes nothing; not the minority's same-price protection but the trigger and whose clock sets it, and it is worthless without a buyer, who knows this and prices the drag into the offer.

New money rewrites the old paper: any term that bites only through an outside arrival can be made a condition of the arrival, so the new lead demands the ratchet waived, the stack collapsed, pay-to-play imposed, or every earlier preferred converted to common at a fraction, and the old terms are worth at most what the arrival is worth to their holders, as in the recapitalization that turns three rounds of preferences into common in one afternoon; not a term but the state that reprices terms, and the true counterparty of a state-contingent power is whoever supplies the state.

Successor in the chair: a term is held by an entity and exercised by whoever the entity has become when the state arrives, so the veto priced against a friendly partner is pulled by that partner's replacement, by a fund in wind-down that needs distributions, by a secondary buyer who took the position at a discount and breaks even at a different price, or by a continuation vehicle with a fresh clock, as the drag that was a courtesy at signing and a sale order twelve years later; not the term but the replacement of its holder, and the counterparty of the term was never the counterparty of the negotiation.

source.register: Operator-grade and concrete: preferences, ratchets, vetoes, drags, thresholds, and seats as they appear in United States venture preferred-stock documents, with two Delaware decisions (ThoughtWorks on redemption, Trados on the preferred's director) and the fund's own life cycle as the remote domain that sharpens the last two items.
source.mode: Analytical distinctions with observed illustrative cases, each simplified to one mechanism; the recapitalization and the successor cases are readings of a common practice rather than of a named dispute, and the thesis that terms are mispriced in proportion to the distance of their biting state is an authored interpretation carried by the seriation, not a measurement.
source.via: practice-deep-ideonomy; two Fable fieldwork breaths; independent Fable editorial review
boundary_claim: Authored fieldwork on the United States venture form set, chiefly NVCA-style preferred stock; not a survey of every term, not a legal opinion, and the same handle can bite differently under another draft or another jurisdiction.

The mispricing thesis is an interpretation: the seriation is an itinerary of how much must change from the day of signing before a term bites, not a measured scale of mispricing, and no empirical claim about which terms parties misprice is made.

The illustrative cases (ThoughtWorks, Trados, the eleventh-month firing, the recapitalization, the fund past its tenth year) are simplified to expose one mechanism each and are not accounts of the specific histories.
Price itself is outside: valuation, the pre-money option pool, discounts, and caps, and every route by which ownership drains other than through a power in a state, belong to another map.
Debt covenants, warrants, and the fund's own partnership terms are outside except as cases; Successor in the chair points at fund-level terms without mapping them.

seriation.axis: How much must change from the day of signing before the term bites: nothing but the calendar (a dividend accrues, a redemption date arrives, a threshold is crossed by arithmetic), then the company's own fortunes (the middling exit, the flat band, the split syndicate, the conflicted seat, the decline seen first, the founder's sale, the founder's firing), then an outside arrival (the party whose speed prices the veto, the next round, the down round, the rescuer, the buyer), and finally the parties themselves (the arrival that rewrites the paper, the holder who is replaced).
seriation.note: An authored itinerary, not a ranking of severity or a scale of mispricing. Dividend in the drawer opens it because nobody and nothing need change for it to bite; Successor in the chair closes it because the party exercising the term is no longer the party who priced it. The route's interpretive claim is that the further along it a term sits, the less anyone at the table rehearses its state, which is the live question answered as an itinerary rather than as a finding. Claim on the middle → Flat where the founder is steep is the first teaching adjacency: the claim says where the preferred is paid, the flatness says where it stops caring, and between them lies the band in which the investor's vote is for the sale and the founder's is against it. New money rewrites the old paper → Successor in the chair is the hinge: once a term bites only through an arrival, the arrival can rewrite it, and once the holder is replaced, the term is exercised by someone who never priced it, so the last two stops are where the signer neither supplies the state nor holds the power, and every earlier stop is repriced from there.

exploration.first_question: Which terms in a financing carry power beyond their price, in which future state does each bite, who holds the power then, and in which case did the term prove worthless or fatal? And which of them are priced by the parties who sign them?
exploration.changed_question: Breath one assumed each term is exercised as written in its state. Sharpening the ratchet, the redemption right, and the class veto against their own states showed that each is unusable as written in exactly the state it was written for (the ratchet kills the round it protects against, the redemption demands cash the law will not release, the veto delays a rescue the vetoing class also needs), so each is cashed as consent, the price of its waiver, paid by whoever must supply the state. The question moved to: who supplies the state in which a term bites, and who holds the term when it arrives? Both answers name parties who are never in the room at signing, the new money whose arrival triggers the state and can rewrite the paper as a condition of arriving, and the successor who holds the term after the partner, the fund, or the position has changed hands. The pointer's title stands; the of-sentence now includes waiver-only terms and unsigning holders.
exploration.new_member: New money rewrites the old paper: any term that bites only through an outside arrival can be made a condition of the arrival, so the new lead demands the ratchet waived, the stack collapsed, pay-to-play imposed, or every earlier preferred converted to common at a fraction, and the old terms are worth at most what the arrival is worth to their holders, as in the recapitalization that turns three rounds of preferences into common in one afternoon; not a term but the state that reprices terms, and the true counterparty of a state-contingent power is whoever supplies the state.

priorities.item: Flat where the founder is steep: in the band where the preferred's payoff is flat, from the preference up to the conversion point for non-participating stock and from the cap up to it for capped participation, the preferred gains nothing from a higher price while the common's payoff is at its steepest, so a holder with a vote on the sale prefers the certain offer now to a better one later, as when the investors accept an acquirer's price inside the flat band and the founders, whose every extra dollar would be theirs, are dragged; not the size of the claim but its slope, and an uncapped participating preferred has the claim without the flatness.
priorities.why: It is arithmetic on a cap table rather than a reading of documents, so it can be checked on any real company in an hour; and it names the modal disagreement over a sale, which founders experience as a difference of ambition when it is a difference of slope.
priorities.next_question: Take one real cap table with two or three series, compute each holder's payoff slope at every exit value from zero to the last conversion point, and mark the bands in which a holder with a sale vote has zero slope; then list every acquisition offer the company received and ask which offers fell inside a flat band, and whether those were the offers the investors urged accepting.

priorities.item: Successor in the chair: a term is held by an entity and exercised by whoever the entity has become when the state arrives, so the veto priced against a friendly partner is pulled by that partner's replacement, by a fund in wind-down that needs distributions, by a secondary buyer who took the position at a discount and breaks even at a different price, or by a continuation vehicle with a fresh clock, as the drag that was a courtesy at signing and a sale order twelve years later; not the term but the replacement of its holder, and the counterparty of the term was never the counterparty of the negotiation.
priorities.why: Low plausibility that it can be priced at signing, high generative promise: it asks whether any state-contingent term can be priced without a model of who its holder will be in that state, which turns the term sheet into a question about the fund's partnership agreement, and nobody negotiates one against the other.
priorities.next_question: For one company's cap table, list each term's holder as of signing and as of today (partner in the seat, fund year, secondary transfers, continuation vehicles, key-person events) and mark the terms whose effective holder changed; then ask which of those terms was priced against the original holder's clock, and whether a single clause (a consent right over transfers of the preferred, a sunset on the veto at fund year ten) would have kept the term with the party who priced it.

gate.standard: declared type, close-neighbor discriminator, boundary case, and form inference

neighbors.left: Claim on the middle: a one-times non-participating preference exists only for exits between the preference and the point where converting to common pays more, since at the top it converts and adds nothing and at zero it is a claim on nothing, as the stack of preferences that exceeds a company's realistic sale price leaves the common underwater and makes the acquirer buy the management back with a carve-out plan; not downside protection, which would pay at the bottom, but a claim on the modal exit that nobody at signing rehearses.
neighbors.right: Flat where the founder is steep: in the band where the preferred's payoff is flat, from the preference up to the conversion point for non-participating stock and from the cap up to it for capped participation, the preferred gains nothing from a higher price while the common's payoff is at its steepest, so a holder with a vote on the sale prefers the certain offer now to a better one later, as when the investors accept an acquirer's price inside the flat band and the founders, whose every extra dollar would be theirs, are dragged; not the size of the claim but its slope, and an uncapped participating preferred has the claim without the flatness.
neighbors.separating_case: An uncapped participating preferred: it holds a claim in the middling exit, taking its preference and then its share, so Claim on the middle is present; but its payoff rises with every dollar of price, so there is no band in which its holder stops caring, and Flat where the founder is steep is absent. Conversely a one-times non-participating preferred is flat from the preference to the conversion point. Participation keeps the claim and removes the flatness, which pulls the two mechanisms apart: one is where the claim exists, the other is where its slope is zero.

checks.boundary_case: The pre-money option pool, sized by the investor and counted in the pre-money so the founders alone are diluted by it, is a tempting member: it moves ownership without a vote and bites in a state the founder did not picture (a pool left unissued at exit). It is out because it has no state in which it does anything other than lower the effective price; it is price in disguise, and belongs to a map of ownership drains. Registration rights fail from the other side: there is no state in which they bite that the underwriters do not control, so they are a fossil at signing rather than a power.
checks.form_inference: The map shows a fork the sequence conceals: Option on the next round's information and Reserves test in loyalty's clothing sit at different stops but draw on the same reserve in opposite states, so a fund cannot fully hold both without dry powder kept for both weathers. It shows two passages between levels: Ratchet that must be waived → New money rewrites the old paper, where a term over the founder becomes a chip against whoever supplies its state, and Veto priced by the clock → Successor in the chair, where the term passes from its wording to its holder. It shows a loop: First to know it is dying → Pass that stamps the sale, where the information lag spoils the outsider's price and returns as the insiders' own mark. It shows a claim recruiting a duty against its own holder at Claim on the middle → Chair that owes the room, and a dependency at Stack that sorts the syndicate → Threshold that ends independence, where the drag's counting rule decides whose split preference governs. And New money rewrites the old paper → Threshold that quietly disenfranchises shows the last stop of the itinerary reaching back to reprice the first, which no line can draw.
checks.target_preserved: Self-read only. Each item names a term, the state in which it bites, the holder in that state, and a case where it was worthless or fatal; the strange members (a claim on the middle that buys back the management it stripped, a term whose whole value is its own waiver, a seat that is a liability in the state it was taken for, a refusal read as a price, a holder who never signed) are kept as mechanisms rather than softened into advice about negotiating better terms.
